section_summary: This section comprises U.S. Embassy monthly political reports from Tokyo and State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs memoranda from July through October 1933. The documents cover Japanese domestic politics, notably Seiyukai-Cabinet tensions, budget battles, the public trials of the League of Blood and May 15 assassins, and newly thwarted ultranationalist coup plots. Foreign affairs coverage focuses on negotiations over the sale of the Chinese Eastern Railway, Sino-Japanese tensions in North China and Chahar, commercial negotiations with Great Britain and India at Simla and London, and diplomatic friction surrounding American naval expansion and police-stoked 'spy scares.'

subfiles.about: Concluding portion of the monthly report on political, economic, and international conditions in Japan during June 1933, including diplomatic lists and a formal summary.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This document represents the final section of Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 459, concluding the review of June 1933 and providing lists of despatches and telegrams followed by a three-page summary. It details preparations for the Simla and London trade conferences with the British Empire, negotiations in Tokyo for the sale of the Chinese Eastern Railway to Manchukuo, discussions concerning extraterritoriality in Manchukuo, and Sino-Japanese developments after the Tangku Truce. In domestic affairs, it analyses internal Seiyukai factional splits over supporting Premier Saito, the political rivalries of Generals Ugaki and Araki, plans to build up the Japanese Navy to London Treaty limits, and economic trends including dollar depreciation and easy credit. Additional topics cover the ideological renunciation of communism by Gaku Sano and Sadachika Nabeyama, academic freedom disputes at Kyoto University resulting in the dismissal of Professor Takikawa, and the disruption of a morphine smuggling operation in Nagasaki.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 459: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of June, 1933

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum reviewing and highlighting key points of Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 490 (July 1933 monthly political report).
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum evaluates Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 490 covering July 1933. It calls particular attention to the opposition voiced by General Kunishige Tanaka and the Meirinkai society against the military's economic policies in Manchuria, noting Tanaka's prominent conservative background and his advocacy for private capital investment. The memo also comments on Japanese plans to make Tsingtao a premier commercial terminus via continental rail extensions into Shaanxi and Gansu, analyzes why the anti-British trade agitation lost momentum among the Japanese public and military, and notes French commercial diplomacy and Japanese approval of an Afghan minister.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum: Tokyo's Despatch No. 490 Transmitting the Monthly Report for July 1933

subfiles.about: Comprehensive monthly political and economic report on Japan for July 1933, transmitting detailed analysis of foreign relations, domestic politics, assassinations, and commerce.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Transmitted by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew under Despatch No. 490, this complete monthly report covers Japanese developments in July 1933, including a table of contents, lists of despatches and telegrams, and duplicate pages of the opening section. Foreign affairs reporting reviews police-generated espionage allegations against American Embassy Physician Dr. Rudolf B. Teusler and Army Language Officer Lieutenant J. R. Sherr, press criticism of American naval expansion, deadlocked Chinese Eastern Railway negotiations in Tokyo, and frontier friction with Soviet border guards. It also covers the death of Field Marshal Muto and appointment of General Hishikari in Manchukuo, Japanese protests against Western loans to China and Dr. Rajchman's League mission, Marshal Feng Yuxiang's military activities in Chahar, and preparations for trade talks at Simla and London. In internal politics, the report highlights the public trials of civilian, military, and naval perpetrators of the 1932 assassinations, the arrest of over 100 Dai Nihon Seisanto conspirators plotting an armed coup, severe drought damage to the rice crop, and the creation of a Foreign Office Trade Commission.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 490: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of July, 1933

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum reviewing Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 510 regarding Japanese internal and foreign affairs during August 1933.
subfiles.summary: This internal memorandum from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes and comments upon Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 510 of September 5, 1933. It assesses Japanese police actions against American citizens such as Langston Hughes, Upton Close, and Alex H. Buckman, agreeing with the Embassy that these exclusions stemmed from anti-radical and anti-pacifist vigilance rather than specific anti-American animus, as demonstrated by identical treatment given to European leftists like Lord Marley. The memorandum also evaluates conciliatory public statements toward the United States by War Minister Sadao Araki and Count Uchida as deliberate tactical efforts to condition American opinion favorably ahead of the upcoming 1935 naval treaty conference, while noting military sensitivity surrounding T. V. Soong's return to China.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum: Tokyo's Monthly Report for August 1933 (Despatch No. 510)

subfiles.about: Monthly political report on Japan for August 1933, detailing Japanese-American relations, naval rumors, police expulsions, and goodwill diplomatic maneuvers.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This despatch comprises the transmittal cover sheet, table of contents, and initial sections of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report on conditions in Japan for August 1933. It details persistent police vigilance and sensational vernacular press rumors concerning alleged secret American naval bases in Magdalena Bay, Mexico, and Fukien Province, China, as well as alleged U.S. contracts to train Chinese aviators. The text reviews police actions barring or expelling radical or pacifist visitors, including American author Upton Close, African American writer Langston Hughes, Harold Isaacs, Alex H. Buckman, British peer Lord Marley, and Belgian delegate Dr. Albert Marteaux. It contrasts this popular suspicion with calculated friendly gestures by high Japanese officials, citing War Minister Sadao Araki's interview with Kent Cooper of the Associated Press and Prince Iyesato Tokugawa's goodwill journey to America, interpreting both as efforts to disarm American suspicions and lay groundwork for Japan's demands for higher ratios at the next naval conference.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 510: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of August, 1933
